source.title: Isolated Mononeuropathy From Rucksack Palsy: A Case Series

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Primary case-series findings were atomized at case-level granularity. Key secondary synthesis claims in the discussion and Table II were retained with secondary_synthesis or secondary_reported_result tags. Bibliographic entries were not atomized.

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary aim was to describe the clinical patterns of isolated spinal accessory and long thoracic mononeuropathies attributed to rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The primary aim of this case series is to introduce the clinical patterns of isolated mononeuropathies involving the SAN and the LTN secondary to rucksack palsy.

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary aims were to emphasize education about improper rucksack use and safety features relevant to rucksack design.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The secondary aims include illustrating the need for education on the risks of improper rucksack use and highlighting the safety features to improve the modern rucksack.

atoms.canonical_statement: The case series presents three military personnel with isolated mononeuropathy attributed to rucksack use, one involving the spinal accessory nerve and two involving the long thoracic nerve.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Three cases of mononeuropathy secondary to rucksack use in military personnel are presented, including injuries to the long thoracic and spinal accessory nerves.

population.label: Three military personnel with rucksack-associated mononeuropathy

atoms.canonical_statement: The article reports all three cases individually and summarizes their clinical features, nerve conduction studies, electromyography findings, and diagnoses in Table I.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All cases have been reported below. Additionally, Table I gives a summary snapshot of each case, whereas Table II gives a summary of Rucksack palsy.

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 was a 29-year-old active duty male soldier, 5 ft 10 in and 210 lb, diagnosed with left spinal accessory neuropathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 1 Male Muscular Height: 5′ 10” Weight: 210 lbs Left Spinal Accessory Neuropathy

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 reported frequent body armor and rucksack carriage during military duties in the period when progressive symptoms developed.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: during a period in which he frequently wore body armor and carried rucksacks for his military occupation.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

exposures.details: Frequent occupational use during symptom development

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 developed generalized left shoulder and periscapular pain with weakness during shrugging exercises, with an insidious course over about five years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A 29-year-old active duty male soldier presented with generalized left shoulder and periscapular pain, as well as weakness with shrugging exercises.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 had left upper trapezius atrophy and lateral scapular winging; nerve conduction testing showed a markedly reduced left spinal accessory nerve CMAP relative to the right, and trapezius EMG showed mildly reduced recruitment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: nerve conduction study (NCS) demonstrated markedly reduced left SAN compound motor action potential relative to the contralateral side.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors diagnosed chronic, incomplete left spinal accessory neuropathy in case 1.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A diagnosis of chronic, incomplete, left spinal accessory neuropathy was made.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 underwent ultrasound-guided hydrodissection of the left spinal accessory nerve.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The patient subsequently underwent ultrasound-guided hydrodissection of the left SAN

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

concept.text: Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection of the left spinal accessory nerve

atoms.canonical_statement: After spinal accessory nerve hydrodissection, case 1 had good pain relief, continued his military occupation, and had no documented later encounters for left shoulder symptoms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: with good pain relief. He has since continued with his military occupation, with no documented encounters for left shoulder symptoms thereafter.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 was a 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman, 6 ft 1 in and 215 lb, diagnosed with right long thoracic neuropathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 2 Male Muscular Height: 6′ 01” Weight: 215 lbs Right Long Thoracic Neuropathy

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 symptoms began after a 13-mile ruck march while training overseas with an older internal-frame rucksack loaded to 65 lb.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: His symptoms began following a 13-mile ruck march while training overseas. He reported using an older model rucksack with an internal frame, which was loaded with 65 pounds.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

concept.text: Ruck march with loaded older internal-frame rucksack

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 presented after two months of right scapular winging, push-up weakness, and mild nonneuropathic right shoulder pain.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: presented with a two-month history of right scapular winging and weakness with push-ups, as well as mild, nonneuropathic right shoulder pain.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 had right medial scapular winging; EMG showed spontaneous activity in the right serratus anterior without findings of right brachial plexopathy, and the right trapezius and rhomboid were normal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A subsequent electrodiagnostic study revealed spontaneous activity in right serratus anterior, no findings of right brachial plexopathy, and a normal right trapezius and rhomboid on EMG.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors diagnosed right incomplete long thoracic neuropathy in case 2.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A diagnosis of a right, incomplete, long thoracic neuropathy was made.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 received nonsurgical treatment with physical therapy, dry needling, and relative rest.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: He was treated nonsurgically with physical therapy, dry needling, and relative rest.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: At five months after injury, case 2 could perform 91 push-ups, although he still reported disproportionate right-sided fatigue during push-ups.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: at five months postinjury, he was able to perform 91 push-ups, but continued to feel his right-side fatigue disproportionately during push-ups.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

quantitative_result.original_result_text: at five months postinjury, he was able to perform 91 push-ups

atoms.canonical_statement: At one year after injury, case 2 was pain free and passed the Navy SEAL screener.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: At one-year postinjury, he was completely pain free and he successfully passed the rigorous Navy SEAL screener.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 was a 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger, 6 ft 1 in and 205 lb, diagnosed with left long thoracic neuropathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 3 Male Muscular Height: 6′ 01” Weight: 205 lbs Left Long Thoracic Neuropathy

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 developed symptoms after prolonged rucksack marches during a field training course.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: presented with a three-month history of left shoulder weakness following prolonged rucksack marches at a field training course.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

concept.text: Prolonged rucksack marches during field training

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 reported left shoulder weakness, greatest with overhead movement, plus mild generalized nonneuropathic shoulder pain; examination showed active flexion and abduction limited to 90 degrees with preserved passive motion and medial scapular winging.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: His examination was notable for inability to actively flex or abduct his left shoulder beyond 90 degrees. Passive range of motion was preserved.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 EMG of the left serratus anterior showed abnormal spontaneous activity and reduced motor unit recruitment, while nerve conduction testing showed markedly reduced left long thoracic nerve CMAP relative to the right.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: EMG of the left serratus anterior revealed abnormal spontaneous activity and reduced motor unit recruitment.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors diagnosed left incomplete long thoracic neuropathy in case 3.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A diagnosis of left, incomplete long thoracic neuropathy was made.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: At nine months, follow-up EMG in case 3 showed serratus anterior reinnervation and normalization of motor unit recruitment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Follow-up EMG of the left serratus anterior nine months later showed evidence of reinnervation and normalization of his motor unit recruitment pattern.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: At eight months, case 3 could perform more than 53 push-ups.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: At eight months postinjury, he was able to perform over 53 push-ups.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: By 17 months, case 3 had returned to full military duty without restrictions but still could not effectively perform weighted overhead presses.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: By 17 months, he had returned to full military duty without restrictions, although he remained unable to effectively do weighted overhead presses

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 reported that most trainees used the hip belt only on marches longer than one hour; cases 2 and 3 used older-model rucksacks, and hip-belt use for those cases was unavailable.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: one soldier (case 3) reported that during training most trainees would only use their hip belt on marches longer than one hour in length.

atoms.canonical_statement: The article defines rucksack palsy as compression or traction injury to the brachial plexus or surrounding nerves caused by prolonged shoulder-region load.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A condition where a prolonged load over the shoulder region results in a compression or traction injury to the brachial plexus or surrounding nerves.

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II lists prolonged shoulder load, improper strap positioning or donning, older or frameless rucksacks, heavy loads, and thin body habitus as risk factors for rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Risk Factors 1. Prolonged load on shoulder

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II lists weakness, scapular winging, shoulder or periscapular pain, and upper-extremity paresthesia as manifestations of rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Manifestations 1. Upper extremity weakness 2. Scapular winging 3. Shoulder or periscapular pain 4. Upper extremity paresthesia

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II lists brachial plexopathy, mononeuropathy, cervical radiculopathy, primary shoulder pain, a space-occupying lesion, and thoracic outlet syndrome in the differential diagnosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Differential Diagnosis 1. Brachial plexopathy 2. Mononeuropathy 3. Cervical radiculopathy

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II summarizes management as stopping provocative activity, allowing time for neuropraxic recovery, physical therapy to restore biomechanics, and selective surgical neurolysis for severe cases.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Management 1. Cessation of provocative activities

atoms.canonical_statement: The discussion cites prior work estimating annual rucksack palsy incidence in military personnel at 29.7 to 53.7 per 100,000.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the incidence of rucksack palsy among service members has been estimated to be between 29.7 and 53.7 per 100,000

atoms.canonical_statement: The discussion reports a 1987 study with annual rucksack paralysis incidence of 0.157 per 1000 soldiers using a framed pack and 1.17 per 1000 using a pack without a frame.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 0.157 per 1000 soldiers (0.0157%) using a pack with a frame and 1.17 per 1000 soldiers (0.117%) using a pack without a frame

atoms.canonical_statement: The discussion reports biomechanical work in which anatomically modeled backpack straps produced four times lower subclavian artery strain and 50% lower skin stress than a standard strap.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: anatomically modeled straps produced four times lower strain on the subclavian artery and 50% lower skin stresses compared with the standard strap.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that isolated mononeuropathy from rucksack use is under-recognized and most commonly affects the long thoracic and spinal accessory nerves.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Isolated mononeuropathy secondary to rucksack use is an under-recognized condition and most commonly affects the LTN and SAN.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors recommend further evaluation, including electrodiagnostic testing, when rucksack use is associated with scapular winging.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A history of rucksack use in association with scapular winging should warrant further evaluation, including electrodiagnostic examination.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that education for active-duty personnel about rucksack risks may prevent cases of rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: With proper education for active duty soldiers in operational and training environments, many cases of rucksack palsy may be prevented.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that greater provider awareness of rucksack palsy clinical patterns may improve recognition and treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: increasing awareness among providers regarding the different clinical patterns of rucksack palsy may assist in the recognition and treatment of these conditions.

atoms.canonical_statement: The article states that most conclusions about the superiority of modern rucksack designs are anecdotal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: most of the conclusions on superiority are anecdotal.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that more research is needed to determine which modern rucksack is most effective at preventing rucksack palsy and to identify other protective design factors.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: More research is needed to conclude which modern rucksack is most effective in preventing rucksack palsy.
